Banded iron formations, the striped rocks in which layers rich in iron oxide alternate with layers of chert, were deposited in ancient oceans for more than a billion years and then largely ceased to form. For decades geologists treated them as a straightforward record of early photosynthesis: oxygen released by cyanobacteria, the argument ran, reacted with dissolved ferrous iron, and the insoluble oxides that resulted rained down onto the seafloor. On this reading, the abundance of the formations measured the rising productivity of oxygen-producing microbes, and their disappearance marked the moment when the oceans had been swept clean of dissolved iron.

The tidiness of this account has not survived closer scrutiny. Laboratory cultures have shown that certain bacteria can oxidize iron without producing any oxygen at all, using light to strip electrons directly from ferrous iron. If such organisms flourished in the early oceans, the formations could have accumulated in waters that were entirely anoxic, and their presence would say nothing about when oxygen-producing photosynthesis began. A third camp has proposed that ultraviolet radiation, unfiltered by an ozone layer that did not yet exist, could have oxidized surface iron with no biological help, though experiments simulating realistic seawater chemistry suggest that this process would have been too slow to account for the thickest deposits.

It would be premature, however, to conclude that the formations are uninformative. Iron isotopes fractionate differently depending on the pathway by which iron is oxidized, and several research groups now argue that the isotopic signatures of particular layers can discriminate among the competing mechanisms. The difficulty is that diagenesis, the slow chemical alteration that sediments undergo after burial, can shift those signatures in ways that are themselves poorly constrained. The rocks, in other words, may contain the answer, but only in a script whose grammar has been partly rewritten by time. What seems clear is that the formations cannot be read as a single uniform archive; different deposits, laid down in different basins and epochs, may record different processes, and the older habit of generalizing from one well-studied sequence to the entire record now looks less like parsimony than like wishful simplification.

Economic historians long regarded the craft guilds of late medieval Europe as brakes on innovation. By fixing prices, restricting entry and dictating the methods by which goods could be made, guilds supposedly protected their members' incomes at the expense of consumers and inventors alike. Adam Smith's hostility to such corporations gave this view an intellectual pedigree, and it fitted comfortably into a narrative in which economic growth began only when markets were freed from corporate privilege.

A revisionist literature has complicated this picture without wholly overturning it. Its proponents point out that the apprenticeship system, which guilds regulated, was the principal means by which tacit technical knowledge passed between generations in an age with few written manuals. Because a guild could enforce the obligations of both master and apprentice, it made long training contracts credible: masters could expect years of cheap labor in return for instruction, and apprentices could expect that the instruction would actually be given. Moreover, journeymen who traveled from town to town before settling, a practice many guilds encouraged or required, carried techniques across regions and may have done more to diffuse innovations than any patent system of the period.

Critics of the revisionists concede the importance of apprenticeship but question whether guilds were necessary to sustain it. Training contracts were also enforced by municipal courts and by families with reputations to protect, and in several prosperous towns apprenticeship flourished where guilds were weak. The critics further note that the documentary record is skewed: guild statutes survive in abundance precisely because guilds were record-keeping bodies, while informal arrangements left few traces, so a historian reading the archive may mistake the visibility of guild regulation for its indispensability.

The disagreement thus turns less on what guilds did than on what would have happened in their absence, a counterfactual that no archive can directly answer. Both sides would probably accept that guilds were neither uniformly obstructive nor uniformly beneficial, and that their effects varied with the trade, the town and the century in question.

The epistolary novel, which tells its story entirely through letters, enjoyed a vogue in eighteenth-century Europe that critics have often explained by appeal to its apparent immediacy. Because each letter is written, or purports to be written, in the heat of the moment, the form seems to offer unmediated access to a character's feelings as they arise, before retrospection has had a chance to tidy them. Readers of the period, so the argument goes, prized this effect of sincerity, and novelists cultivated it by insisting in their prefaces that they were merely the editors of a genuine correspondence.

This account captures something real, but it neglects a feature of the form that its most accomplished practitioners exploited with evident relish: the letter is never addressed to no one. Every letter is shaped by its writer's sense of a particular recipient, and a character who confides in a friend will present events differently from the way she presents them to a parent or a suitor. Far from guaranteeing sincerity, the form therefore invites the reader to compare versions, to notice what is emphasized for one correspondent and suppressed for another, and to infer a truth that no single letter states. The immediacy the form promises is, on this view, precisely what it teaches the reader to distrust.

One need not conclude that eighteenth-century readers were naive in taking the letters at face value, for the evidence of their responses is mixed. Some contemporary readers wrote to authors in distress over the fates of characters, as though the correspondence were genuine; others, in reviews and private notes, remarked with amusement on the self-serving rhetoric of particular letter writers. What the mixed evidence suggests is not that one reading was correct and the other mistaken, but that the form sustained both at once. A novel in letters could be consumed as a sequence of sincere outpourings and, simultaneously or on a second reading, as a study in the strategic management of sincerity. That doubleness, rather than immediacy alone, may best account for the form's appeal, and for its decline once novelists found other means, such as the free indirect style, of letting readers glimpse a gap between what characters say and what they mean.

Botanists have reported for some years that certain plants appear to treat their relatives differently from strangers. In a frequently cited greenhouse study, seedlings of a beach-dwelling annual grew fewer fine roots when potted with siblings than when potted with unrelated plants of the same species, as though competing less vigorously against kin. Subsequent work has described similar effects in several other species, and some researchers now speak of kin recognition in plants as an established phenomenon, attributing it to chemical cues released by roots.

Skeptics have raised two objections, one methodological and one conceptual. The methodological objection concerns how root allocation is measured. Plants potted with siblings are, by definition, more similar to one another in size and growth rate than plants potted with strangers, and size asymmetries alone can alter how much a plant invests in roots. Unless an experiment controls for such asymmetries, a difference attributed to recognition may simply reflect the fact that evenly matched neighbors compete differently from mismatched ones. Several reanalyses that adjusted for plant size found that the apparent kin effect shrank, and in some cases vanished.

The conceptual objection is subtler. To say that a plant recognizes kin is to imply that it detects relatedness as such, rather than responding to some correlate of relatedness, such as genetic similarity at a few loci that happen to govern root exudates. Defenders reply, reasonably enough, that recognition in animals is also mediated by correlates, since no organism perceives genealogy directly; a ground squirrel that distinguishes siblings by odor is responding to chemistry, not to pedigree. If the term is acceptable for the squirrel, they ask, why not for the sunflower?

The reply has force, but it does not settle the matter, because the animal cases are persuasive for reasons that go beyond the existence of a cue. In those cases, discrimination has been shown to produce behavior that benefits relatives at some cost to the actor, which is what evolutionary theory predicts kin recognition should do. For most plant studies, that demonstration is still missing: a plant that grows fewer roots near siblings may be conserving resources for itself rather than ceding them to kin. Until such costs and benefits are measured, the more cautious description, that plants respond differently to neighbors of differing relatedness, seems the one the evidence supports.

That workers in large cities earn more than otherwise similar workers in small towns is one of the most robust findings in urban economics. The difference is usually attributed to agglomeration economies: when many firms and workers cluster together, they share suppliers, draw on a deep pool of specialized labor and learn from one another, and these advantages raise productivity enough to pay for the higher wages and rents that dense places impose. On this interpretation, the urban wage premium is a measure of something that cities create.

A persistent difficulty is that the workers who move to cities are not a random sample of the population. If more able or more ambitious workers sort into large cities, part of the wage premium reflects who lives there rather than what the city does for them. Economists have tried to separate these effects by following individual workers as they move. Studies of this kind generally find that a worker who moves to a large city does not receive the full premium at once; instead, her wage rises gradually over the following years and, strikingly, much of the gain persists if she later moves back to a smaller place.

This pattern has been read in two ways. Some take it as evidence that cities foster the accumulation of skills, so that the premium reflects learning that workers carry with them. Others caution that the workers who move to a city, stay for several years and then leave may differ systematically from those who never move or who stay permanently, and that the persistence of their gains could reflect selection operating at a second stage. The first reading treats the city as a school; the second warns that we may be observing only the school's most promising pupils.

The choice between these readings matters for policy. If the premium arises mainly from learning, then subsidizing access to large cities, for instance by easing the housing restrictions that keep rents high, could raise the productivity of workers who would otherwise never benefit. If the premium is largely a matter of sorting, such measures would chiefly reshuffle where productive workers live without making anyone more productive. Current evidence leans toward a substantial role for learning, but the second-stage selection problem has not been convincingly ruled out.

For much of the twentieth century, art historians approached Dutch still-life painting of the seventeenth century as a repository of hidden meanings. A peeled lemon, a guttering candle, a watch lying open beside a half-eaten pie: each object, it was argued, belonged to a vocabulary of moral emblems familiar to contemporary viewers, who would have recognized in such arrangements a meditation on the transience of earthly pleasure. Scholars who adopted this approach, often called iconographic, assembled impressive evidence from emblem books of the period, in which images of everyday things were paired with verses drawing exactly such lessons.

Beginning in the 1980s, a number of scholars objected that the iconographic method had become self-confirming. Almost any object could be matched with some emblem, and once a painting was assumed to carry a message, the absence of explicit cues could be explained away as subtlety. The critics proposed instead that the paintings be understood in relation to the commercial culture that produced them: as luxury goods made for an expanding market of urban buyers, who valued them for their dazzling imitation of textures and for the costly imported objects they depicted. A Chinese porcelain bowl, on this account, signaled the reach of Dutch trade rather than the fragility of life.

It is tempting to treat these as rival interpretations between which one must choose, but the opposition may be less stark than either camp has supposed. The emblem books themselves were commercial products, sold to the same urban public that bought paintings, and their popularity suggests that buyers enjoyed precisely the oscillation between delight in things and reflection on their vanity. A painting that rendered a silver goblet with astonishing skill could at once flatter its owner's taste and remind him, if he cared to be reminded, that such possessions would not outlast him. To insist that the painting meant only one of these things is to impose a coherence that the culture may not have demanded.

This reconciliation has its own risk, of course. If every painting can be read both ways, the claim becomes difficult to test. The more productive course may be to ask, of particular works, which reading the specific choices of the painter make more probable.

The discovery in the 1990s of gas giant planets orbiting their stars in a matter of days posed an immediate puzzle. Theories of planet formation, built largely to explain our own solar system, held that giant planets could assemble only far from their stars, beyond the so-called snow line, where ices are abundant enough to build massive solid cores quickly. A Jupiter-sized planet circling its star at a small fraction of Mercury's distance therefore seemed to require that the planet had formed farther out and then moved inward.

Two migration mechanisms have been proposed. In disk migration, a young planet exchanges angular momentum with the gas disk from which it formed and spirals gradually inward, a process that would leave its orbit nearly circular and aligned with the star's equator. In high-eccentricity migration, gravitational interactions with other planets or with a companion star fling the planet onto an elongated orbit whose closest approach brings it near the star, where tidal forces then shrink and circularize the orbit over hundreds of millions of years. Because this second process begins with a violent perturbation, it would often leave the orbit tilted relative to the star's spin.

Measurements of that tilt have accordingly been treated as a test between the mechanisms. Many hot Jupiters do turn out to have strongly misaligned orbits, a result initially welcomed as support for high-eccentricity migration. Yet the inference is less secure than it first appeared. The star's spin axis may itself be tilted relative to the disk, through processes unrelated to the planet, so that even a planet that migrated smoothly through the disk could end up misaligned with its star. Conversely, tides raised by a massive planet might, around some kinds of stars, gradually realign an orbit that had begun tilted.

Meanwhile, a once-neglected alternative has gained ground: that some hot Jupiters formed where we find them. Simulations suggest that, under certain conditions, solids could drift inward and accumulate close to the star rapidly enough to build a core before the gas disk dissipates. No one claims that this possibility explains every case. Its advocates argue more modestly that the population of hot Jupiters may be heterogeneous, the product of several pathways, and that searching for a single mechanism may have been a mistake from the start.

Creole languages, which arise when speakers of different languages are brought together in circumstances that demand a new common tongue, have long attracted linguists interested in how grammar emerges. Two broad accounts have dominated the debate. Substrate theorists hold that a creole's grammar is inherited largely from the languages its first speakers already knew: although most of the vocabulary may come from the socially dominant language, the underlying structures, such as how tense is marked or how questions are formed, are carried over from the speakers' native languages. Universalists counter that creoles across the world share features, such as preverbal markers of tense and aspect, that cannot be traced to any single set of source languages, and that these shared features reveal a default grammar that human beings produce when inherited models are unavailable.

Each position faces difficulties. The universalist argument depends on the claim that the similarities among creoles exceed what common sources would explain, yet many well-studied creoles drew on related source languages, so that resemblances between them may reflect shared inheritance after all. The substrate argument, for its part, struggles with cases in which a creole possesses a construction found in none of the languages known to have contributed to it. Substrate theorists can reply that our knowledge of which languages were present is often incomplete, but this reply, however plausible in particular cases, risks becoming an all-purpose escape.

More recent work has tended to dissolve the dichotomy rather than resolve it. Researchers who examine the social history of particular colonies have found that the demographic conditions under which creoles formed varied enormously, from settings in which a few source languages were spoken by large, stable groups to settings in which constant turnover prevented any group from transmitting its grammar. On this view, the relative weight of inheritance and invention is not a constant to be discovered but a variable that depends on such conditions. Creoles that emerged where a single substrate predominated should show more substrate influence; those that emerged amid extreme linguistic diversity might show more of the features universalists emphasize. Whether the evidence bears out these predictions is still being examined, but the reframing has at least made the question empirically tractable.

The movement known as historically informed performance, which seeks to play older music on the instruments and in the styles of its own era, began in the mid-twentieth century as a marginal enterprise and has since become something close to an orthodoxy in the performance of Baroque repertory. Its early advocates presented it as a corrective to a romanticized tradition that had smothered the music of Bach and Handel under massed strings and sentimental tempos. By recovering gut strings, period wind instruments and the evidence of contemporary treatises, they claimed, performers could hear the music as its composers had intended.

The most searching criticism of the movement has come not from defenders of the older style but from scholars sympathetic to its results. They have pointed out that the treatises on which performers rely are fragmentary, often contradictory and frequently prescriptive rather than descriptive: a writer who complains that singers ornament too lavishly tells us what he disliked, not necessarily what was usual. More fundamentally, the critics argue that the goal of reproducing the composer's intentions is incoherent, since even a perfect reconstruction of an eighteenth-century performance would be heard by listeners whose ears have been shaped by two further centuries of music. The sound might be authentic; the experience could not be.

The sharpest of these critics went further, contending that historically informed performance was less a recovery of the past than an expression of modern taste. The lean textures, brisk tempos and rhythmic clarity that its practitioners favored, they observed, bore a suspicious resemblance to the aesthetic of twentieth-century modernism, with its distrust of romantic excess. The movement, on this reading, had not escaped the habit of remaking old music in the image of the present; it had merely exchanged one present for another.

That argument is more illuminating than its tone sometimes suggested. It need not imply that the movement's achievements are spurious. Performers who have learned to play period instruments have discovered sonorities and balances that no amount of reading could have revealed, and many listeners find the resulting performances more vivid than what preceded them. What the criticism undermines is not the value of these performances but the claim of authority that once accompanied them: they are persuasive interpretations, not recoveries of a single correct sound.

The idea that predators at the top of a food web can reshape entire ecosystems, a phenomenon ecologists call a trophic cascade, gained wide currency through studies of rocky shores and lakes in the 1960s and 1970s. Removing a predatory starfish from a stretch of shoreline, for instance, allowed mussels to monopolize the rock and crowd out dozens of other species. Such experiments were persuasive in part because the systems were small and the interventions could be replicated and reversed.

Extending the concept to large terrestrial landscapes has proved more contentious. When a top predator returns to a region from which it had long been absent, ecologists often report changes at lower levels of the web: herbivores become warier, browsing declines in certain areas, and plants long suppressed begin to recover. It is natural to read these changes as a cascade set in motion by the predator. Yet in such landscapes the predator's return rarely occurs in isolation. Herbivore populations may also be shrinking because of hunting by people, competition from other grazers or a run of severe winters; rainfall and stream flow may be shifting; and plant recovery may lag years behind any of these causes, making it hard to say which one it is following.

The disagreement is not merely about data but about what would count as adequate evidence. Proponents of a strong cascade argue that convergent patterns across many sites, each imperfect on its own, make the predator's role the most economical explanation. Skeptics reply that convergence is only as informative as the independence of the sites, and that many of the landscapes studied share climate trends and management histories that could produce similar patterns without any predator effect at all. They favor approaches, such as fencing plots to exclude herbivores, that isolate one causal link at a time, even though such experiments cannot capture the indirect effects of fear that cascade theorists consider important.

Neither side, it seems fair to say, has a monopoly on rigor. Small-scale exclusion experiments establish mechanisms cleanly but may misrepresent how those mechanisms operate across a landscape; broad comparisons capture the landscape but blur the mechanisms. The most defensible conclusions so far are likely to be modest ones: predators can contribute to vegetation recovery, but the magnitude of their contribution probably varies from place to place.

Why people in several parts of the world began to cultivate plants, a practice that at first seems to have demanded more labor for less nutrition than foraging, remains one of archaeology's enduring questions. For much of the twentieth century the dominant answers invoked necessity: a warming climate, a growing population or the depletion of large game, it was argued, pressed communities to intensify their use of plants until cultivation became unavoidable. Such accounts had the virtue of explaining why a costly innovation was adopted, but they predicted that the earliest farmers should show signs of nutritional stress, and in several regions the skeletal evidence has proved equivocal.

An alternative proposal, sometimes called the feasting hypothesis, shifts attention from subsistence to social life. On this view, ambitious individuals in relatively prosperous foraging societies sponsored communal feasts in order to accumulate prestige and obligations, and the demand for foods suitable for feasting, especially grains that could be brewed into beer, encouraged the deliberate tending of particular plants. Cultivation would thus have begun not as a response to scarcity but as a by-product of competition for status under conditions of relative abundance. Excavations at some early sites have uncovered large stone vessels and the remains of what appear to be communal gatherings, which proponents cite in support.

The hypothesis has attracted interest partly because it explains a puzzle that necessity-based accounts leave untouched: why the first cultivated plants in some regions were not the most calorie-efficient ones available. Yet its evidential basis is thinner than its explanatory appeal. Residues that would confirm brewing are difficult to distinguish from those left by other forms of food preparation, and large gatherings could have served purposes, such as ritual or the exchange of marriage partners, that had nothing to do with competitive display. Moreover, the hypothesis requires that feasting precede cultivation at the sites in question, and the dating of the relevant layers is often too coarse to establish the order.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of the debate is that the transition need not have had a single cause. Social motives may have initiated the tending of certain plants in some places, while climatic and demographic pressures later turned a marginal practice into a way of life.

Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in accounts of scientific knowledge. A physicist who imagines riding alongside a beam of light, or a philosopher who asks what would follow if a person's memories were transferred to another body, performs no measurement and gathers no new data. Yet such imagined scenarios have, by the testimony of scientists themselves, sometimes reshaped entire fields. The question is how reasoning about situations that never occur can teach us anything about the world.

One influential answer holds that thought experiments are simply arguments in picturesque dress. On this deflationary view, any genuine conclusion a thought experiment yields can be reconstructed as an explicit argument from stated premises, and the imagined scenario contributes nothing beyond making the argument vivid and memorable. Whatever we learn, we learn because the premises were already known, perhaps tacitly, and the reasoning from them is valid. The view has the merit of demystifying the practice: it requires no special faculty of insight, only ordinary inference.

Critics object that the deflationary view misdescribes how thought experiments actually function. They point out that a well-constructed scenario often reveals a tension among beliefs that the thinker did not realize were in conflict, and that the premises needed to reconstruct the argument become visible only after the scenario has done its work. A reconstruction may thus be possible in retrospect without capturing how the knowledge was acquired. Some critics go further and claim that certain thought experiments give us direct insight into laws of nature, though this stronger claim has found few adherents, since it seems to grant the imagination an authority that its frequent failures do not warrant.

The more modest criticism seems to me to have the better of the argument, but it concedes more to the deflationist than its proponents sometimes acknowledge. To say that a scenario brings latent assumptions to light is to grant that the knowledge was, in some sense, already present; the scenario's contribution is to make it available for scrutiny. That contribution is real, and it is not trivial, since a great deal of intellectual progress consists in noticing what one already believes. But it is a contribution to the organization of knowledge rather than a new source of it.

For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists held that the adult mammalian brain produced no new neurons. The doctrine began to erode in the 1960s, when researchers reported newly generated cells in the brains of adult rats, and it collapsed in the 1990s as studies in rodents and primates documented the steady birth of neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory. A widely cited study of tissue from adult human patients then appeared to confirm that the same process occurs in people, and adult neurogenesis was quickly incorporated into accounts of learning, mood and the effects of exercise.

In recent years the consensus has fractured. Several laboratories examining postmortem human brains have reported that markers of immature neurons, abundant in children, become vanishingly rare in the adult hippocampus, while others, using similar markers, report substantial numbers well into old age. The discrepancy has prompted a dispute about technique as much as biology. The proteins used to identify young neurons degrade at different rates after death, and their detection depends on how quickly tissue is preserved and how it is treated chemically. Groups that find few new neurons argue that their opponents have mistaken other cell types for immature neurons; groups that find many reply that the skeptics' samples were preserved too slowly for the fragile markers to survive.

Each side's methodological criticism has some merit, which is precisely what makes the question hard to settle. Postmortem tissue cannot reveal whether a cell was born recently, only whether it displays features associated with youth, and those features may not be unique to newborn neurons. Methods that do track cell birth directly, such as measuring the carbon isotopes incorporated into DNA, have been applied to humans, but they require assumptions about cell turnover that critics consider questionable.

None of this implies that the rodent findings were mistaken; neurogenesis in the rodent hippocampus is among the best-replicated results in the field. The open question is how far those findings transfer to a species whose brain develops more slowly and lives far longer. It may turn out that adult humans produce new hippocampal neurons, but at rates too low to bear the functional weight that popular accounts have placed on them.

Few ideas in social psychology spread as quickly beyond the discipline as the claim that self-control draws on a limited resource. In the experiments that launched it, participants who first performed a task requiring restraint, such as resisting a plate of cookies, gave up sooner on a subsequent unsolvable puzzle than participants who had not been asked to exercise restraint. The effect, named ego depletion, was soon reported in hundreds of studies using a bewildering variety of initial and subsequent tasks, and it was invoked to explain everything from dieting failures to poor decisions late in the day.

The sheer number of supporting studies once seemed decisive. In retrospect, it was part of the problem. Many of the studies were small, and the flexibility of the paradigm, in which almost any effortful task could serve as the depleting manipulation and almost any measure of persistence as the outcome, gave researchers wide latitude in how to analyze and report their data. Under such conditions, a literature can accumulate many positive results even if the underlying effect is weak or absent, because studies that find nothing are less likely to be published. When several large, coordinated replication efforts were finally conducted, each following a protocol fixed in advance, the effects they found were close to zero.

Defenders of the theory have not abandoned it. Some argue that the replication protocols used manipulations too mild to deplete anyone, and that the original effect will reappear with stronger tasks. Others suggest that depletion depends on participants' beliefs: people who think willpower is limited behave as though it is, while those who think otherwise do not. Critics respond that each such amendment makes the theory harder to refute, since any failure can now be attributed to an insufficiently strong manipulation or to the wrong beliefs.

Whatever the eventual verdict, the episode has become an object lesson in how a research field can generate an impressive body of evidence for an effect that may be much smaller than it appeared. Its lasting contribution may lie less in what it revealed about self-control than in the reforms, such as preregistration and large collaborative replications, that it helped bring about.

How the builders of Gothic cathedrals knew that their soaring vaults and slender piers would stand has puzzled historians of architecture for well over a century. The masons of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries possessed no theory of structural mechanics in the modern sense; the mathematics needed to calculate the thrust of a vault was not developed until several hundred years later. Nineteenth-century writers, impressed by the apparent daring of the buildings, sometimes concluded that their designers must have possessed an intuitive genius for structure, a gift that allowed them to sense where forces would travel through stone.

Later scholars found this explanation unsatisfying, not least because it explained everything and therefore nothing. They proposed instead that Gothic design rested on rules of proportion transmitted within the masons' lodges: geometric procedures, such as deriving the thickness of a buttress from a fraction of the span of the vault it supported, that had proved reliable in earlier buildings and were passed on through apprenticeship. Such rules required no understanding of why they worked. Their success depended on a convenient property of masonry, whose strength is governed far more by geometry than by the absolute size of a structure, so that a shape that stood at one scale would usually stand when enlarged.

The proportional account is better supported by the surviving documents, which include drawings and a few written rules, than the appeal to genius ever was. It nonetheless leaves something out. The documents record procedures, not the process by which those procedures were first arrived at, and some of the most ambitious buildings went beyond anything their predecessors had attempted. Here the record also contains failures: vaults that collapsed during construction, towers that had to be taken down, choirs rebuilt after their supports gave way. These episodes suggest that the rules were refined through a long and sometimes costly process of trial, observation and correction, in which builders watched cracks open in mortar and adjusted their designs accordingly.

Gothic construction, on this view, was neither the work of solitary genius nor the mechanical application of inherited formulas. It was an empirical tradition, cumulative and fallible, whose knowledge resided less in any individual than in the accumulated experience of the lodges.

Many of the molecules on which life depends can exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, much as a left hand mirrors a right. In the laboratory, ordinary chemical reactions that produce such molecules generally yield the two forms in equal amounts. Living organisms, by contrast, are strikingly one-sided: the amino acids in their proteins are almost exclusively of the left-handed form, and the sugars in their nucleic acids almost exclusively right-handed. Explaining how this uniformity, called homochirality, arose from a presumably balanced prebiotic chemistry is a central problem in research on the origin of life.

Proposed explanations divide roughly into two groups. The first holds that some physical asymmetry in the environment favored one form slightly over the other. Circularly polarized light, which occurs in certain regions of space, can destroy one mirror form a little faster than the other, and some meteorites contain amino acids with a modest excess of the left-handed form, which suggests that such processes may have operated before Earth formed. The second group of explanations holds that the initial bias could have been purely a matter of chance, since any finite collection of molecules will contain slightly unequal numbers of the two forms by random fluctuation alone.

Either kind of explanation faces the same further difficulty: the excesses it can produce are small, often a few percent at most, whereas biology requires something close to purity. Attention has therefore shifted to mechanisms of amplification, chemical processes in which a slight initial imbalance is magnified. Several have been demonstrated. In one, a reaction product catalyzes its own formation while inhibiting the formation of its mirror image, so that whichever form gains an early lead quickly dominates. In another, crystals that are repeatedly ground and dissolved convert gradually to a single form.

These demonstrations show that amplification is chemically possible, but they leave open whether any of them could have operated under the conditions of the early Earth, many relying on reagents or procedures unlikely to have occurred naturally. They also blunt the significance of the original debate. If amplification is powerful enough, a tiny bias of either origin would suffice, and the meteoritic evidence, however intriguing, would not by itself show that life's handedness was determined in space.

Why the Industrial Revolution began in eighteenth-century Britain rather than elsewhere is a question that economic historians have answered in many ways, invoking coal deposits, colonial markets, secure property rights and a culture receptive to science. One influential recent answer focuses on relative prices. British wages, it is argued, were unusually high by international standards, while British coal was unusually cheap. Under these conditions, machines that substituted energy and capital for labor were profitable in Britain at a time when the same machines would have lost money in regions where labor was cheap and fuel dear. The early spinning machines and steam engines, on this view, were invented in Britain because it was the only place where it paid to invent them.

The high-wage hypothesis has the appeal of explaining not merely that inventions occurred but why they took the particular labor-saving form they did. It also accounts for a pattern that otherwise seems odd: several key British machines were adopted slowly abroad, even after their designs were widely known. If the machines were profitable only at British prices, their slow diffusion is just what one would expect until engineers had made them more efficient.

Critics have challenged the hypothesis on both empirical and theoretical grounds. Empirically, the comparison of wages depends heavily on how one converts earnings across currencies and on which occupations and regions are compared; some recalculations find British wages less exceptional than the hypothesis requires. Theoretically, high wages raise the payoff from saving labor but do not by themselves explain why British inventors, rather than those elsewhere, possessed the skills to build the machines. Some critics therefore argue that the supply of capable mechanics and instrument makers, rather than the demand created by relative prices, was the decisive factor.

The two explanations are less opposed than their proponents sometimes imply. Incentives to invent matter little without people able to respond to them, and a reservoir of mechanical skill would have produced few labor-saving machines in an economy where saving labor did not pay. A complete account will probably require both, together with an explanation of why Britain possessed each.

In the 1930s, a young American classicist studying the Homeric epics proposed that their most conspicuous stylistic feature, the recurrence of fixed phrases such as "swift-footed Achilles" and "rosy-fingered Dawn", was not a mark of literary mannerism but evidence of how the poems were made. The phrases, he argued, fitted the meter so precisely, and were distributed so systematically by grammatical case and metrical position, that they must have formed a traditional system that enabled poets to compose aloud in performance. Fieldwork among singers of heroic songs in the Balkans, who improvised long narratives using similar stock phrases, seemed to confirm that such composition was possible.

The oral-formulaic theory transformed Homeric studies, but it also generated a difficulty its founders did not fully anticipate. If the formulas were chosen for metrical convenience, it seemed to follow that they carried little meaning in context. A hero might be called "blameless" at a moment when he was behaving badly, simply because the epithet fitted the line. Some scholars drew the conclusion that it was a mistake to read Homeric diction with the attention to nuance that critics bring to written poetry, since apparent ironies might be accidents of the system.

This conclusion has been resisted from several directions. Some scholars have shown that the poems frequently depart from the formulaic system, substituting an unusual phrase where a standard one was available, and that such departures often coincide with dramatically significant moments. Others argue that even a standard epithet need not be meaningless, since an audience steeped in the tradition would hear in each use an echo of the hero's role across many songs, a resonance that a single literary text could not supply. On this view, traditional diction is not the opposite of meaning but a different way of producing it.

The disagreement has implications beyond Homer. It bears on how we read any literature that emerged from a tradition of performance, and on whether interpretive methods developed for printed texts can be transferred to works whose original audiences experienced them very differently. The answer is likely to vary with the work, but the question can no longer be ignored.

Roughly thirteen thousand years ago, as the last ice age was ending, much of the Northern Hemisphere plunged abruptly back into near-glacial cold. The episode, known as the Younger Dryas, lasted about twelve centuries before warming resumed, and in places the temperature changes at its beginning and end appear to have unfolded within a few decades. Such speed is difficult to reconcile with the slow orbital variations that pace the ice ages, and explaining it has become a test case for theories of abrupt climate change.

The most widely accepted explanation involves the circulation of the North Atlantic. Warm surface water flowing northward releases heat to the atmosphere, cools, grows denser and sinks, drawing more warm water behind it. If enough fresh water floods the surface, the water may become too buoyant to sink, weakening the circulation and cooling the regions it warms. Proponents argue that the draining of a vast glacial lake into the ocean supplied the necessary fresh water. The mechanism is physically well understood, and sediment cores record a weakening of the circulation at about the right time.

The difficulty has been to establish the route and timing of the flood. Early versions of the hypothesis assumed that the lake drained eastward into the North Atlantic, but geological surveys along that route long failed to find unambiguous evidence of a flood of the right age. More recent work suggests that the water may instead have escaped northward through the Arctic, a path from which it could still have reached the regions where deep water forms. Critics regard this shift as a rescue of the hypothesis rather than a confirmation; proponents reply that revising a route in light of better data is simply how geology proceeds.

A few researchers have proposed an entirely different trigger, such as the impact of a comet fragment, but this proposal has persuaded comparatively few specialists, partly because the evidence offered for it has proved difficult to reproduce. The circulation mechanism, by contrast, is accepted even by many who doubt the particular flood story: abrupt shifts of the kind seen in the Younger Dryas appear repeatedly in the climate record, and a mechanism that can account for the whole family of events seems preferable to one tailored to a single case.

Few historical claims are repeated as confidently as the claim that the printing press transformed European culture. In an influential study published in the late 1970s, one historian argued that the shift from scribal copying to print did more than make books cheaper: by producing large numbers of identical copies, print made it possible for scholars in different cities to refer to the same page, compare editions and correct errors cumulatively. Standardization and preservation, rather than mere quantity, were on this view the press's decisive contributions, and they helped make possible both the religious controversies and the scientific developments of the following centuries.

Later historians have qualified this account in ways that its author did not entirely welcome. Close study of early printed books has shown that copies of the same edition were often far from identical, since corrections were made while sheets were being printed and uncorrected sheets were bound alongside corrected ones. Pirated editions, careless reprints and deliberate alterations were common. The stability that the earlier account attributed to print, these critics argue, was not a property of the technology but an achievement that had to be produced, slowly and imperfectly, through the labor of editors, the reputations of printers and the development of conventions for distinguishing authoritative texts from unreliable ones.

The disagreement is sometimes described as a choice between treating technology as a cause and treating it as a tool shaped by its users. That description is too simple. The critics do not deny that print mattered; they argue that its effects depended on social arrangements that took generations to emerge and that varied from one place to another. Nor did the earlier account claim that the press acted alone, although its emphasis on the inherent properties of print invited that reading.

What the debate has clarified is that standardization is better understood as a historical process than as an immediate consequence of a new machine. The press created possibilities that scribal culture could not easily offer, but whether and how quickly those possibilities were realized depended on choices that the machine did not dictate.

When a honeybee worker returns to the hive after finding a good source of food, she often performs a series of movements on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. In the most famous of these, the waggle dance, the bee runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run, sometimes dozens of times. Other bees crowd around her, following her movements closely, and many of them soon leave the hive and fly toward the food she has found.

In the middle of the twentieth century, an Austrian scientist showed that the dance contains information about where the food is. The direction of the straight run, measured against the vertical, matches the direction of the food measured against the position of the sun. A run pointing straight up the comb means that the food lies in the direction of the sun; a run pointing to the right of vertical means that the food lies the same angle to the right of the sun. The length of each run, in turn, is related to the distance of the food: the farther away the food, the longer the bee waggles.

For some years, other researchers questioned whether bees actually used this information. They pointed out that a returning forager also carries the scent of the flowers she has visited, and that bees following her might simply search for that scent rather than read the dance. The question was finally settled by experiments in which researchers built small robotic bees that performed dances without carrying any scent. Bees that followed the robots flew in the direction the robots had indicated, which showed that the dance itself could guide them.

Scientists now believe that bees use both kinds of information. The dance points recruits toward the general area of the food, and scent helps them find the exact flowers once they arrive. This combination allows a colony to send many workers quickly to a rich source of food, even one that is several kilometers away.

Until the second half of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest over the local church or town hall, and because the sun reaches that point earlier in the east than in the west, clocks in neighboring towns could differ by several minutes. For most people this mattered very little. A farmer or shopkeeper rarely needed to coordinate an appointment with someone thirty miles away, and travel was slow enough that a few minutes' difference passed unnoticed.

The railways changed this. A train that left one town at a scheduled hour and arrived at another needed a timetable that both stations could read in the same way, and when a single line passed through dozens of towns, each with its own noon, the timetables became confusing and, on single-track lines, potentially dangerous. Railway companies responded by adopting a single time for all their stations, usually that of a major city on the line. For a period, many stations displayed two clocks, one showing railway time and one showing local time, and travelers had to keep both in mind.

It is often said that the railways imposed standard time on a reluctant public, and there is some truth in the claim. Some towns resisted giving up their local noon, and in a few places the dispute reached the courts. Yet the story of imposition is incomplete. Many businesses, especially those that depended on the telegraph, found a common time convenient and adopted railway time well before any law required it. In several countries, official standard time was established by legislation only after most of the population had already begun using it. The law, in these cases, confirmed a change that had largely taken place.

The adoption of standard time is therefore better understood as a gradual convergence than as a sudden decree. Railways provided the strongest reason for change, but the habits of businesses and ordinary people determined how quickly the change spread.

Theorists of literary translation have long organized their disputes around a single opposition. A translator may, in one formulation, either leave the author in peace and move the reader toward him, or leave the reader in peace and move the author toward the reader. The first strategy, now usually called foreignization, preserves features of the source text that will strike readers of the translation as unfamiliar: its syntax, its idioms, its allusions to customs the reader does not share. The second, domestication, renders the text in a fluent idiom that reads as though it had been written in the reader's own language, smoothing away whatever might impede comprehension.

In recent decades a number of critics have championed foreignization on ethical grounds. Fluent translations, they argue, make the translator invisible and conceal the cultural difference of the original, assimilating foreign works to the expectations of a dominant readership. A translation that retains some strangeness, by contrast, reminds readers that they are encountering another culture on its own terms. The argument has been influential, and it has encouraged translators to resist the assumption that a good translation is one in which no trace of translation can be detected.

Yet the opposition on which the argument rests is less stable than it appears. What counts as foreign depends on the reader: a construction that seems exotic to one generation may seem merely old-fashioned to the next, and a translation that preserves the source's syntax may strike readers less as an encounter with another culture than as clumsy prose. Moreover, the features a translator chooses to preserve are themselves selected according to the translator's assumptions about what is characteristic of the source culture, so that foreignization can produce not the other culture as it is but a stylized image of its otherness. Domestication, meanwhile, need not erase difference; a fluent translation can convey unfamiliar ideas and values while presenting them in familiar sentences.

None of this makes the ethical concern misguided. It suggests rather that the concern cannot be satisfied by a stylistic policy applied in advance. Whether a translation respects the difference of its source is a question to be asked of particular choices in particular texts, not one settled by allegiance to either side of a dichotomy.
